content: CD90, also known as Thy-1, is a highly conserved cell surface protein that is heavily N-glycosylated and anchored to the cell membrane via a glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI) linkage. It has a molecular weight of 25–37 kDa and contains a single V-like immunoglobulin domain. Initially identified as a thymocyte antigen, Thy-1 serves as a marker for various stem cells and the axonal processes of mature neurons. Its structural study contributed to the foundation of the immunoglobulin superfamily and provided early insights into the biochemical characterization of GPI anchors and tissue-specific glycosylation. Discovery and Nomenclature Thy-1 was the first T-cell marker to be identified. It was discovered in 1964 by Reif and Allen during their search for heterologous antisera against mouse leukemia cells. They demonstrated its presence on murine thymocytes, T lymphocytes, and neuronal cells. Initially named the theta (θ) antigen, it was later renamed Thy-1 (Thymocyte differentiation antigen 1) due to its identification in thymocytes. The human homolog of Thy-1 was isolated in 1980 as a 25 kDa protein (p25) from the T-lymphoblastoid cell line MOLT-3. The discovery of Thy-1 in mice and humans paved the way for identifying other T-cell markers, which are critical to understanding the adaptive immune response. Gene Conservation and Alleles The Thy-1 gene is highly conserved across vertebrates and some invertebrates, with homologs identified in species such as squid, frogs, chickens, mice, rats, dogs, and humans. In humans, the Thy-1 gene is located on chromosome 11q22.3, while in mice, it is found on chromosome 9qA5.1. The gene is closely situated to CD3 and CD56/NCAM genes, suggesting potential functional significance. In mice, there are two alleles of Thy-1: Thy1.1 (Thy-1a, CD90.1) and Thy1.2 (Thy-1b, CD90.2), which differ by a single amino acid at position 108 (arginine in Thy1.1 and glutamine in Thy1.2). Most mouse strains express Thy1.2, while strains like AKR/J and PL express Thy1.1. Protein Structure The core protein of rodent Thy-1 is 25 kDa in size and consists of 111 or 112 amino acids, excluding its heavy glycosylation. It is N-glycosylated at three sites, whereas human Thy-1 has only two glycosylation sites. The Thy-1 precursor protein contains a 19-amino-acid signal sequence and a 31-amino-acid C-terminal transmembrane domain, which is removed during the transfer of the mature peptide to the GPI anchor. Common monoclonal antibodies used to detect Thy-1 include clones OX7, 5E10, K117, and L127. Some Thy-1 monoclonal antibodies have been reported to cross-react with cytoskeletal elements, such as actin and vimentin, due to sequence homology. Thy-1, like other GPI-anchored proteins, can be shed by phospholipase C enzymes, such as PI-PLC, and can participate in the cell-to-cell transfer of GPI-anchored proteins like CD55 and CD59. Glycosylation Thy-1 is one of the most heavily glycosylated membrane proteins, with carbohydrates accounting for up to 30% of its molecular mass. It has three N-glycosylation sites (Asn23, Asn74, and Asn98) but no O-glycosylation. The glycosylation pattern of Thy-1 varies between tissues and even among cells of the same lineage at different stages of differentiation. For example, brain Thy-1 contains galactosamine, while thymic Thy-1 has a higher sialic acid content, which increases with T-cell maturation. Thy-1 was the first glycoprotein in which cell-type-specific glycosylation on an invariant protein was demonstrated. The glycosylation core pattern includes oligomannose structures at Asn23, extended complex structures at Asn74, and smaller complex structures at Asn98. Expression Thy-1 expression varies across species and cell types. It is expressed on thymocytes, neurons, mesenchymal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, NK cells, endothelial cells, renal glomerular mesangial cells, metastatic melanoma cells, follicular dendritic cells, fibroblasts, and myofibroblasts. In mice, Thy-1 is found on thymocytes, peripheral T cells, myoblasts, epidermal cells, and keratinocytes. In humans, it is expressed on endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, CD34+ bone marrow cells, umbilical cord blood cells, cardiac fibroblasts, and fetal liver-derived hematopoietic cells. In the nervous system, Thy-1 is predominantly expressed on neurons, with some glial cells also expressing it during later stages of differentiation. Thy-1 expression in the brain is developmentally regulated, with low levels in neonatal brains that increase during postnatal development. Localization As a GPI-anchored protein, Thy-1 is localized to the outer leaflet of lipid rafts in the cell membrane. In neurons, it is strongly expressed in mature axons, with the axon hillock acting as a barrier to its lateral spread. Thy-1 interacts with G inhibitory proteins, Src family kinases like c-fyn, and tubulin within lipid rafts. In rats and mice, Thy-1 is present on the soma and dendrites of neurons but is not expressed on axons until axonal growth is complete. Thy-1 expression is temporarily suppressed during axonal injury. Thy-1 also co-localizes with the HIV-1 matrix in lipid rafts, facilitating the incorporation of Thy-1 into virus particles during budding. Functions The precise function of Thy-1 remains unclear, but it is implicated in cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, neurite outgrowth, nerve regeneration, apoptosis, metastasis, inflammation, and fibrosis. Role in Cognition Thy-1 knockout mice exhibit normal social interactions and learning in mazes but fail to learn from social cues, such as identifying safe foods based on other mice's behavior. This deficit can be rescued by transgenic Thy-1 expression or treatment with GABA(A) receptor antagonists, suggesting excessive GABAergic inhibition in the dentate gyrus and impaired long-term potentiation. Axon Growth Regulation Crosslinking Thy-1 with antibodies promotes neurite outgrowth via Gαi and calcium channel activation. Thy-1 interacts with β3 integrins, which may halt axon growth during interactions between maturing axons and mature astrocytes. T-Cell Activation In mouse T cells, Thy-1 crosslinking in lipid rafts can substitute for T-cell receptor signaling when combined with strong CD28 costimulation. Conversely, it can substitute for CD28 costimulation during TCR activation. Apoptosis and Necrosis Crosslinking Thy-1 with antibodies induces apoptosis in thymocytes and mesangial cells, despite Bcl-2 upregulation. In mesangial cells, apoptosis is confirmed by TUNEL and annexin V staining, though electron microscopy suggests necrosis. Tumor Suppression Thy-1 acts as a tumor suppressor in certain cancers by upregulating thrombospondin, SPARC, and fibronectin. However, it may also facilitate extravasation in circulating melanoma cells. In prostate cancer, Thy-1 is expressed in cancer-associated stroma but not in normal stroma, making it a potential target for cancer-specific therapies. Fibrosis Modulation Thy-1 plays a role in fibrosis, with tissue-specific variations. In lung fibrosis, Thy-1 expression is suppressed in stimulated fibroblasts. Thy-1 knockout mice exhibit increased lung fibrosis, including fibrosis induced by bleomycin. Use in Stem Cell Biology Thy-1 is a marker for various stem cells, including hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), mesenchymal stem cells, hepatic stem cells, and keratinocyte stem cells. In humans, Thy-1 is co-expressed with CD34 on HSCs and is considered a marker of pluripotency.
